html:
After the school bell rings, many children in Wardha and nearby villages return home without textbooks, tutors, or quiet space to study. After-school learning fills that gap — and it is one of the most practical ways an NGO can support long-term education outcomes.

Published by the Lata Agrawal Foundation in Wardha, Maharashtra. Read more at https://agrawalfoundation.org/blog/why-after-school-learning-matters-for-village-children-in-wardha/.

The gap between school and home

Government schools do essential work, but large class sizes and limited resources mean children often need extra help with reading, maths, and homework. Without it, bright students can fall behind simply because no one at home can explain a lesson again.

Community learning spaces — even a shaded veranda with donated books — give children a safe place to revise, ask questions, and build confidence. Programs like the Lata Agrawal Foundation learning library connect families to free online tools such as Khan Academy.

What effective support looks like

Strong after-school programs combine three things: a regular schedule, trained volunteers or teachers, and materials matched to the child's grade. Snacks or a simple meal can dramatically improve attendance when families worry about hunger.

Tracking attendance and basic learning milestones — not expensive tests — helps NGOs adjust quickly. Small cohorts of 15–20 children per mentor often work better than one-off mega events.

How families and donors can help

Donors can sponsor notebooks, lamps for evening study, or internet access for a community centre. Volunteers can commit to one hour weekly for reading practice — consistency matters more than expertise.

If you are in Wardha, visit our contact page to explore tutoring, book drives, or computer-centre support. Every sustained hour of learning compounds over a child's school years.

title: More Than a Checkup: Restoring Smiles and Confidence
excerpt: What if something as simple as a dental checkup could change the way someone smiles — and the way they feel about themselves? At Sewashram Wardha, this became a reality on 13th April 2024, when Lata Agrawal Foundation organized a free dental camp for children and young adults. For many, this wasn’t just another health
html:
What if something as simple as a dental checkup could change the way someone smiles — and the way they feel about themselves?

At Sewashram Wardha, this became a reality on 13th April 2024, when Lata Agrawal Foundation organized a free dental camp for children and young adults.

For many, this wasn’t just another health visit. It was their first time receiving proper dental care. Some came in quietly, unsure of what to expect. Others carried the discomfort they had learned to live with.

But as the day unfolded, something changed. Fear turned into ease. Uncertainty turned into trust. And most importantly, hesitant expressions turned into genuine smiles.

Because this initiative was never just about dental care.It was about dignity, care, and being seen. It was about reminding every individual that their health matters, their smile matters, and they matter.

Sometimes, the smallest acts of care can leave the biggest impact — and in this case, it started with a smile.

Credits: Story written by Pauline Muhuyi based on Lata Agrawal Foundation’s work

excerpt: After the school bell rings, many children in Wardha and nearby villages return home without textbooks, tutors, or quiet space to study. After-school learning fills that gap — and it is one of the most practical ways an NGO can support long-term education outcomes. Government schools do essential work, but large class
html:
After the school bell rings, many children in Wardha and nearby villages return home without textbooks, tutors, or quiet space to study. After-school learning fills that gap — and it is one of the most practical ways an NGO can support long-term education outcomes.

Published by the Lata Agrawal Foundation in Wardha, Maharashtra. Read more at https://agrawalfoundation.org/blog/why-after-school-learning-matters-for-village-children-in-wardha-discover-volunteer-opport/.

The gap between school and home

Government schools do essential work, but large class sizes and limited resources mean children often need extra help with reading, maths, and homework. Without it, bright students can fall behind simply because no one at home can explain a lesson again.

Community learning spaces — even a shaded veranda with donated books — give children a safe place to revise, ask questions, and build confidence. Programs like the Lata Agrawal Foundation learning library connect families to free online tools such as Khan Academy.

What effective support looks like

Strong after-school programs combine three things: a regular schedule, trained volunteers or teachers, and materials matched to the child's grade. Snacks or a simple meal can dramatically improve attendance when families worry about hunger.

Tracking attendance and basic learning milestones — not expensive tests — helps NGOs adjust quickly. Small cohorts of 15–20 children per mentor often work better than one-off mega events.

How families and donors can help

Donors can sponsor notebooks, lamps for evening study, or internet access for a community centre. Volunteers can commit to one hour weekly for reading practice — consistency matters more than expertise.

If you are in Wardha, visit our contact page to explore tutoring, book drives, or computer-centre support. Every sustained hour of learning compounds over a child's school years.

title: Why After-School Learning Matters for Village Children in Wardha: Books Youth Education
excerpt: After the school bell rings, many children in Wardha and nearby villages return home without textbooks, tutors, or quiet space to study. After-school learning fills that gap — and it is one of the most practical ways an NGO can support long-term education outcomes. Government schools do essential work, but large class
html:
After the school bell rings, many children in Wardha and nearby villages return home without textbooks, tutors, or quiet space to study. After-school learning fills that gap — and it is one of the most practical ways an NGO can support long-term education outcomes.

Published by the Lata Agrawal Foundation in Wardha, Maharashtra. Read more at https://agrawalfoundation.org/blog/why-after-school-learning-matters-for-village-children-in-wardha-books-youth-education/.

The gap between school and home

Government schools do essential work, but large class sizes and limited resources mean children often need extra help with reading, maths, and homework. Without it, bright students can fall behind simply because no one at home can explain a lesson again.

Community learning spaces — even a shaded veranda with donated books — give children a safe place to revise, ask questions, and build confidence. Programs like the Lata Agrawal Foundation learning library connect families to free online tools such as Khan Academy.

What effective support looks like

Strong after-school programs combine three things: a regular schedule, trained volunteers or teachers, and materials matched to the child's grade. Snacks or a simple meal can dramatically improve attendance when families worry about hunger.

Tracking attendance and basic learning milestones — not expensive tests — helps NGOs adjust quickly. Small cohorts of 15–20 children per mentor often work better than one-off mega events.

How families and donors can help

Donors can sponsor notebooks, lamps for evening study, or internet access for a community centre. Volunteers can commit to one hour weekly for reading practice — consistency matters more than expertise.

If you are in Wardha, visit our contact page to explore tutoring, book drives, or computer-centre support. Every sustained hour of learning compounds over a child's school years.
